texts: At a Spanish café counter, ask politely whether the other speaks Spanish.
You ask someone to repeat what they said.
A friendly opening before you continue in Spanish.
At the cafe counter, you politely ask if Spanish is spoken here.
Hola is the first friendly step in any Spanish scene. It works in the morning, afternoon, and evening.
Morning light in a cafe, an open counter, and a calm first greeting in Spanish.
Mid-exchange, politely ask the other to repeat what they said.
On the street, you ask for the station.
A polite way to hear something again and keep the talk going.
In the middle of the talk, you pause and politely ask for a repeat.
Perdón is the safe A1 word for a small pause or correction. In this service scene it means "sorry" or "pardon," not a big apology.
Soft cafe light, a short pause at the counter, and a calm follow-up question.
On the street, ask politely where the station is.
At the counter, you order a coffee.
A short friendly question about a clear place in town.
On the sidewalk, you stop someone briefly and ask for the station.
Dónde is the key Spanish question word for places. Use it for the station, a cafe, a museum, or a pharmacy.
A bright morning street, a station sign in the distance, and an open asking gesture.
At a Spanish café counter, order a coffee politely.
In a shop, you ask for the price.
A short polite order at the counter, with please clearly included.
At the counter, the order sounds short, calm, and polite.
Café is an easy A1 counter word and a useful cognate for English speakers. The accent mark shows the stress: ca-FE.
A cup on the counter, warm morning light, and a calm order.
In a small shop, ask the price of an item.
At the station, you ask about the departure time.
A direct polite price question for an item in front of you.
In the small shop, you hold the item and ask for the price.
Cuánto is the A1 word for "how much" or "how many." It is the key word for prices and simple amounts.
A small shop, an item on the counter, and a clear price question.
At a station info desk, ask when the train leaves.
At a pharmacy or desk, you ask for help.
What time does the train leave?
A clear question about departure time at the station.
What time does the train leave?
At the station information desk, you ask about the departure time.
Tren means train, not trains. The plural is trenes, so the final n is part of the singular word.
A bright station hall, a departure board in the background, and a calm question at the desk.
At a pharmacy or info desk, ask for help politely.
In small talk, you say something nice about the place.
A short polite request for help, before you name the problem.
In the pharmacy, you walk calmly to the counter and say that you need help.
Ayuda is the direct Spanish word for help. It works in a pharmacy, station, hotel desk, or any simple service moment.
A quiet pharmacy counter, clear light, and a short help request without drama.
Inside a café, make a short positive remark about the place.
While planning, you confirm the time for tomorrow.
A short positive small-talk comment about the place or room.
In the cafe, you turn to the other person and say something nice about the place.
Bonito is a warm A1 praise word for places and things. English may use "nice" here, but bonito can also mean "pretty."
Inside the cafe, warm light, and a short happy look.
At the end of an encounter, confirm a plan for tomorrow at seven.
You close the scene with thanks and goodbye.
A short plan confirmation with a day, a time, and a friendly close.
At the end of the meeting, you casually confirm the plan for tomorrow.
Mañana is a small trap for English speakers: it can mean tomorrow or morning. In this sentence, it means tomorrow.
Late afternoon, a quick handshake or nod, and a calm confirmation.
Close the scene with thanks and a polite goodbye.
A warm close with clear thanks and a friendly goodbye.
As you leave, you turn back for a moment and close the scene warmly.
Gracias is the safe A1 word for thanks in any service scene. Muchas gracias simply makes the thanks stronger.
A door in the background, warm light, and a short thank-you as you leave.
At a small shop or counter, admit you don't understand and ask for help.
You ask someone to write down important information.
I don't understand. Could you help me?
A short polite request for help when something is unclear.
I don't understand. Could you help me?
At the counter, you realize you missed something and calmly ask for help.
Entiendo means "I understand." With no in front, no entiendo is the A1 way to say you do not understand and ask for help.
A small shop in the morning, a brief confused moment, and gentle help from the shop assistant.
At a counter, ask politely to have a name, address, or price written down here.
You ask someone to show you a point on the map.
Could you write it down here, please?
A calm request to write down exact information like a name, address, or price.
Could you write it down here, please?
At the counter, you politely ask for important information to be written down.
Escribir means to write. Use it when you need a name, address, price, or number in writing.
A notepad on the counter, a pen in hand, and important information being written down calmly.
At a counter or sidewalk, ask politely to be shown a location on a map.
You ask which of two options is better.
Could you show me on the map?
A calm request to show a place or point on a map or screen.
Could you show me on the map?
With a map on the counter, you ask someone to show you the point.
Mostrar means to show. It is useful when a place is easier to point to than explain in words.
A city map on the counter, with one finger gently pointing to a spot.
At a shop, ask politely which of two options is better.
You ask if an item is still available.
Which one is better, this one or that one?
A polite choice question between two visible options.
Which one is better, this one or that one?
Two small items sit on the counter, and you ask which choice is better.
Mejor means better and is the simple A1 word for choosing between two options. Este points to this one; ese points to that one.
Two options side by side on the counter, with a calm look from one to the other.
In a small shop, ask politely whether more is available.
You ask if card payment is possible.
A short availability question about whether there is more of an item.
In front of an almost empty shelf, you ask the staff if there is more.
Tiene can mean he or she has, or the polite "do you have?" In a shop, it opens simple availability questions.
A bright shelf with one last item, and a friendly question toward the shop staff.
At the till, ask politely whether card payment is accepted.
A bag and the receipt, please
You ask for a bag and the receipt at the end of a purchase.
A direct question at the till about whether card payment is possible.
At the till, you hold your card ready and ask if card payment works.
Tarjeta is the payment card word in this scene. English speakers should not read it as "target"; at the till, it means card.
A till with a card reader, a card in hand, and a quick look before paying.
A bag and the receipt, please
A bag and the receipt, please
At the till, ask politely for a bag and a receipt with your purchase.
You arrive at a desk with a reservation.
Could I have a bag and the receipt, please?
A short polite request for a bag and receipt at the end of a small purchase.
Could I have a bag and the receipt, please?
While paying, you lift the small items and ask for a bag and the receipt.
Bolsa is the practical shopping word for a bag. It is the thing you ask for at the till when you need to carry your purchase.
Small items on the counter, a bag coming over the edge, and the receipt following.
At a restaurant or counter, announce your arrival with a reservation.
You confirm that this is the right item or choice.
I have a reservation at eight.
You arrive at a host stand or service desk and give your reservation time.
I have a reservation at eight.
At the host stand, you calmly give your reservation time and name.
Reserva is the Spanish noun for a reservation or booking. It is useful when you arrive at a restaurant, hairdresser, or service desk.
A host stand with a reservation book, a quick look at the name, and a calm greeting.
Before committing, confirm politely that this is the correct one.
You ask for a short moment.
A short safety check before you choose an item, bus, or place.
Before stepping forward, you check that this is really the right one.
Correcto means correct or right. In this question, natural English is "the right one," not just "the correct."
Two similar items side by side, with a brief checking moment before the choice.
At a counter, ask the other to wait briefly while you finish a small task.
A calm request for a short moment while you find or finish something.
At the counter, you look in your bag and keep the pause polite.
Momento is the set A1 word in Un momento, por favor. It means moment, not momentum.
A hand in a wallet at the till, a short searching moment, and a calm smile.
On a sidewalk, ask politely whether to turn right or left.
You ask how far it is to walk.
A short polite direction question on the sidewalk.
On the sidewalk, you stop someone briefly and ask about the turn at the next street.
Derecha means right as a direction. Do not mix it with correcto, which means right or correct; the direction pair is derecha and izquierda.
Morning on a quiet street, a quick look toward the next crossing, and a friendly hand gesture.
Mid-navigation, ask politely whether the destination is far.
You check at the door if the place is open.
A short polite distance question before you decide to walk.
Before setting off, you ask if the place is close enough to walk to.
Lejos means far. It pairs with cerca, near, so two small A1 words can answer most distance checks.
A view down the street, the destination far in the background, and a checking pause.
In front of a shop or café, ask politely whether it is currently open.
At the stop, you ask for the right bus line.
A calm question at the door before you go in.
At the door of a small shop, you check the sign and ask to be sure.
Abierto means open as a state, useful for shops, cafes, and museums. It pairs with cerrado, closed.
A doorway in the morning, the sign in focus, and one careful step forward.
At a bus stop, ask politely which bus goes to your destination.
On the bus, you check if your stop is next.
Which bus goes to the center?
A short bus-stop question about which line goes to your destination.
Which bus goes to the center?
At the bus stop, you ask someone which line goes to the center.
Autobús is the Spanish bus word. The accent marks stress on the last syllable: au-to-BUS.
A bus stop with a route map, one finger on the list, and a friendly question.
On a moving bus, confirm whether your stop is coming next.
At the counter, you buy a ticket.
Please, is the next stop mine?
A calm check on the bus to know if your stop is next.
Please, is the next stop mine?
On the bus, you turn briefly and check whether the next stop is yours.
Próxima means next here because parada, stop, is feminine. English says the next stop; Spanish can shorten it to la próxima.
Inside a city bus, a stop display overhead, and a quick question moment.
At a counter, ask politely for a single transit ticket.
You ask about the closing time.
A short friendly ticket request at a counter or machine.
At the counter, you say briefly and politely that you want a ticket.
Billete is the Spain-Spanish word for a travel ticket. It can also mean banknote, so the counter or station context matters.
A station ticket window, a hand passing out a ticket, and a calm exchange.
Outside a shop or museum, ask politely about the closing time.
You ask if the place is on the corner.
A short question about closing time before you plan a visit.
Outside the window, you ask someone leaving about the closing time.
Cierra means it closes. It is the useful A1 form for opening hours, paired with abre, it opens.
A shop window with opening hours, and a quick look at the clock.
On the sidewalk, ask politely whether the destination is on the corner.
You choose together how to go.
Please, is it on the corner?
A calm question about a place that should be on the next street corner.
Please, is it on the corner?
On the sidewalk, you point toward the corner and check if the place is there.
Esquina is the street-corner word for navigation. For an inside corner of a room, Spanish often uses rincón instead.
A street corner in morning light, a finger pointing ahead, and a calm check.
At the end of the night, choose between walking and taking a taxi.
You ask for help after missing your stop.
A casual choice between two ways to go next.
At the end of the evening, you look at each other and choose how to go.
Taxi is international and easy to recognize. In Spanish, en taxi means by taxi, while a pie means on foot.
An evening street with a taxi sign in the background, and two people choosing the next step.
After stepping off late, ask politely for help recovering.
How do I get back to my stop? Could you help me?
A calm help request after you miss your stop and need to recover.
How do I get back to my stop? Could you help me?
You got off one stop too late and calmly ask someone nearby for help.
Parada is the bus or tram stop word. It is not the big station; for trains, estación is usually the station.
A bus stop or platform in late afternoon, with a quick checking look at the route map.
At a restaurant entrance, politely ask for a table.
At the table, you ask for the menu.
A short friendly request for a table at a restaurant or cafe entrance.
At the host stand, you politely ask for a table for two people.
Mesa is the core restaurant word for table. It is feminine, so Spanish says una mesa.
A restaurant entrance in warm evening light, with a host and reservation book.
Seated at a table, politely ask for the menu.
A short polite request for the menu at the table.
You are seated at the table and politely ask the server for the menu.
In Spain, la carta is the restaurant menu. Carta can also mean letter or card, but at a table it means menu.
A restaurant table as the server hands over the menu in a calm exchange.
At a café table or counter, order a tea with a polite marker.
A short polite drink order at the counter or table.
At the counter or table, you briefly say what you would like to drink.
Té means tea. The accent matters: te without the accent is a different small Spanish word.
A cup of steaming tea, warm counter light, and a calm order.
At a café counter, politely refuse sugar on your drink.
You ask if food is fresh.
A short ordering preference where you say no to one ingredient.
While ordering, you politely say you do not want sugar.
Azúcar is the counter word for sugar. Sin azúcar is the fixed A1 phrase for no sugar.
A sugar bowl being moved aside on the counter, with a short friendly gesture.
At a market or counter, ask politely whether the food is fresh.
A short question about whether a food item is fresh.
At the market or counter, you point to the food and ask if it is fresh.
Fresco means fresh for food. English speakers should not read it as a painting style here; at a counter, it is about freshness.
A market display, one finger pointing at the food, and a careful look.
Reply to the server's “anything else?” with a polite close.
You ask to take the order with you.
A polite close after the server asks if you want anything else.
After the server asks if there is anything else, you close the order politely.
Nada means nothing. Nada más, gracias is a clear and polite way to close an order.
A calm counter moment after "anything else?", with warm light and a small smile.
At a café counter, ask politely for the order to be takeaway.
You give a short positive note after eating.
A short polite request to take the order with you.
At the counter, you say briefly that you want the order to go.
Llevar means to take or carry. Para llevar is the fixed Spanish phrase for to go or takeaway.
A cup with a paper lid on the counter, being passed toward the door.
After the meal, give a short positive verdict.
You say something light about the day.
A short casual positive comment after eating or drinking.
After the meal, you turn briefly to the server and give a friendly comment.
Bueno is the basic A1 positive word. Está muy bueno is a natural way to praise food while eating.
An empty plate at the end of the meal, with warm light and a satisfied pause.
In small talk with a server, comment briefly on the day or weather.
You ask for the bill at the end of the meal.
A light small-talk line about the weather while you wait at the counter.
While you wait at the counter, you say something light about the day.
Tiempo can mean weather or time. In hace buen tiempo, it means the weather is nice.
Sun through a cafe window, a look outside, and a light comment between orders.
At the end of the meal, ask politely for the bill.
A short polite request for the bill at the end of the meal.
At the end of the meal, you raise your hand briefly and ask for the bill.
Cuenta is the restaurant bill in this phrase. It can also mean account or count, but la cuenta, por favor means the bill, please.
A table after the meal, a short gesture toward the server, and a calm closing mood.
At a casual appointment, apologize for arriving late.
You admit that you forgot something.
A short casual apology when you arrive after the agreed time.
You arrive at a small casual meeting and briefly apologize for being late.
Tarde can mean late or afternoon. In por llegar tarde, it means arriving late.
A cafe doorway, a quick look at the clock, and a calm sorry gesture.
Mid-conversation, admit you forgot something with a casual fixed expression.
You ask the other person for their name.
I'm sorry, I do not remember it.
A short honest line when you realize you forgot something.
I'm sorry, I do not remember it.
In the middle of the conversation, you realize you forgot something and say it calmly.
Recuerdo means I remember. Use no lo recuerdo as one useful present-tense phrase for I do not remember it.
A short pause in conversation, a small shrug, and an honest calm gesture.
In a casual encounter, ask another person for their name.
You reply warmly after an introduction.
The basic casual question for asking someone their name.
In a casual first meeting, you ask the other person for their name.
Llamas is the tu-form verb in como te llamas. For English speakers, read it as are you called here, not as the animal word llama.
A short open look, a light greeting gesture, and an easy first contact.
After being introduced, reply warmly with the canonical Iberian fixed expression.
You ask where the other person is from.
Nice to meet you. Same here.
A warm fixed reply after someone introduces themself.
Nice to meet you. Same here.
After the introduction, both people answer warmly and keep the meeting friendly.
Gusto is the key word inside mucho gusto, the standard Spanish nice to meet you phrase. It works without choosing a male or female ending.
Two hands in a brief handshake and a friendly look after an introduction.
In a casual chat, ask the other person where they are from.
You check whether the person lives here.
A short casual question about where someone is from.
In early small talk, you casually ask the other person where they are from.
Eres is the everyday tu-form of ser. It opens simple questions about origin, identity, and nationality.
A relaxed table conversation, an interested look, and a simple question.
After the origin question, check whether the person lives locally.
You ask if the person has time tonight.
A short follow-up question about whether the person lives locally.
After asking about origin, you casually check whether the person lives here.
Vives keeps origin and home separate: eres asks where someone is from, while vives asks where they live.
A calm cafe scene, an interested look, and a natural follow-up question.
In a casual social moment, ask whether the other has time tonight.
You suggest a place to meet.
A casual question about whether someone has time this evening.
In a casual afternoon conversation, you ask if tonight could work.
Libre is the simple availability word for plans. It pairs naturally with ocupado, busy.
A terrace in late afternoon light, with an open invitation gesture toward the evening.
Suggest a casual meeting place using the canonical Iberian quedar verb.
You gently move the plan to the next day.
Should we meet at the cafe?
A casual suggestion for meeting at a specific place.
Should we meet at the cafe?
While making plans, you casually suggest a clear meeting place.
we meet / we arrange to meet
In Spain, quedamos is the everyday verb for making plans to meet. It is the natural word for setting up a casual meeting.
A cafe entrance in warm afternoon light, with a friendly gesture toward the meeting place.
Politely postpone a casual plan to the next day.
You close the meeting with a see-you-tomorrow goodbye.
A soft way to move a casual plan to the next day.
You cannot do it today, so you gently move the plan to tomorrow.
Quizás is a soft maybe. It helps you avoid a hard no when you are moving a casual plan.
A half-raised hand, a gentle sideways look, and warm afternoon light.
Close a casual meeting with a “see you tomorrow” goodbye.
A warm casual goodbye with a clear next-day time anchor.
As you leave the meeting, you close with a warm see-you-tomorrow goodbye.
Hasta starts many Spanish goodbye phrases: hasta mañana, hasta luego, and hasta pronto. One word gives you several natural closings.
A door in the background, a small goodbye wave, and warm evening light.
At a pharmacy or hotel desk, say you feel unwell and ask for basic help.
You ask if there is a pharmacy nearby.
I'm sick. Could you help me?
A calm polite line when you feel unwell and need basic help.
I'm sick. Could you help me?
At a pharmacy or reception desk, you calmly say you feel unwell and ask for help.
Enfermo means sick. Spanish uses estar for this temporary state; speakers may change it to enferma when needed.
A pharmacy counter in morning light, with a quiet voice and a helpful gesture from the staff.
On the sidewalk, ask politely whether a pharmacy is nearby.
At the counter, you ask for medicine in a general way.
A short polite question for finding a nearby pharmacy.
On the sidewalk, you ask someone whether there is a pharmacy nearby.
Farmacia is the standard Spain Spanish word for pharmacy. For English speakers, it is close to pharmacy, but the Spanish place is farmacia.
A sidewalk with a green pharmacy cross in the background and a calm question to someone nearby.
At a pharmacy counter, ask in a general way for a medicine.
You point to where it hurts.
A general polite request for medicine at a pharmacy counter.
At the pharmacy counter, you make a simple general request for medicine.
Medicamento is the general word for medicine. It is useful when you do not yet know the exact product name.
A pharmacy counter with drawers behind it and a calm first question.
At a pharmacy or doctor reception, point to a body location and say it hurts.
A short symptom line while pointing to the painful place.
At a pharmacy or doctor reception, you point to the place that hurts.
Me duele is the Spanish pain pattern for it hurts me. English says it hurts here, so learn the Spanish chunk as a whole.
A hand on a shoulder or stomach, a short pain gesture, and a calm consultation mood.
At a pharmacy counter, state a common symptom: headache.
A clear A1 symptom statement for a common headache.
At the pharmacy counter, you calmly name the symptom: a headache.
Cabeza means head. Dolor de cabeza is the Spanish phrase for headache, built as pain of the head.
A hand at the head, a tired pause, and a quiet pharmacy counter.
In a pharmacy, café, or social setting, ask for water politely.
You ask if there is a doctor nearby.
A very short polite request for water.
In a pharmacy or cafe, you briefly and politely ask for water.
Agua means water. Spanish says el agua, but agua is still feminine, so you will hear agua fria and mucha agua.
A glass of water on the counter, a calm handover, and clear midday light.
At a hotel desk or public space, ask politely whether a doctor is nearby.
You tell someone about an allergy.
A calm question about whether a doctor is nearby.
At a hotel desk or pharmacy, you calmly ask whether there is a doctor nearby.
Médico means medical doctor. This phrase asks for nearby help; it is not an emergency-call formula.
A reception counter with a sign for a medical consultation and a calm question.
At a pharmacy, restaurant, or hotel, disclose an allergy.
A clear safety line before food, medicine, or treatment.
At a pharmacy, restaurant, or hotel, you briefly say that you have an allergy.
Alergia is the key safety word. Use alergia a... for allergy to something, such as alergia al polen.
A pharmacy counter or restaurant table, a serious calm look, and a clear explanation.
In a public space, ask another person calmly to call for help.
You close the situation with a warm update.
A calm polite request for another person to get help.
You feel unwell and calmly ask someone to call another person for help.
Llamar can mean call by phone or call someone over. Keep this phrase calm: it asks for help without sounding like an emergency call.
A polite hand gesture, a serious but calm tone, and another person responding.
At the end of a health interaction, say you feel better and thank the helper.
I feel better now. Thank you very much.
A warm closing line after someone helps you.
I feel better now. Thank you very much.
At the end of the help situation, you say that you feel better and thank the helper.
Ya marks a change: now, already, or by now. In ya estoy mejor, it shows that you feel better than before.
Leaving the pharmacy door with a small smile and a grateful look back.
At a station counter, ask for a return ticket.
You ask where the station is.
A clear station-counter request for a round-trip ticket.
At the station ticket window, you briefly ask for a round-trip ticket.
Vuelta means return. In ida y vuelta, it makes the fixed Spanish phrase for a round-trip ticket.
A station ticket window, a hand passing over a round-trip ticket, and a calm exchange.
Near a station, ask politely where it is.
You ask about the departure time.
A polite location question for finding the station.
You calmly ask someone where the station or main stop is.
Estación is the general Spanish word for station. It works for train, metro, and main bus contexts.
A street corner with a station sign in the background and a calm question.
At a station counter or platform, ask the departure time.
A short question about the departure time.
At the counter or on the platform, you ask for the departure time.
Sale is the travel word for leaves or departs. It pairs with llega, arrives.
A departure board and a clock, with a quiet pause before the trip.
On a station platform, confirm this is the right one.
A quick check that you are at the right platform before boarding.
Before boarding, you check whether this is really the right platform.
Andén is the train platform. The accent marks the final stress: andén.
A platform edge with a number sign and a quick check before stepping forward.
On the sidewalk or at a hotel, ask for a taxi.
A direct polite request for a taxi.
At a hotel exit or station forecourt, you briefly ask for a taxi.
Necesito is the direct A1 way to state a need. It is clearer than quiero when you are asking for a service.
A hotel entrance in evening light, a taxi pulling up, and a calm gesture toward the car.
In a shared moment, name where the two of you are heading.
You ask the driver to stop.
A casual line for moving together toward a destination.
With another traveler or in a taxi, you say where you are going next.
Vamos is the we-form of ir and also the everyday Spanish let us go. It is useful for shared movement.
Inside a taxi, a short look forward, and the city moving outside the window.
In a taxi or bus, ask the driver to stop here.
A polite instruction to a driver to stop at this spot.
In a taxi or bus, you politely ask the driver to stop here.
Pare is the polite usted command from parar. Do not confuse pare with para, which means for or in order to.
Inside a taxi, a hand points toward the stop outside the window.
In casual traveler talk or to a driver, name where you are heading.
You ask how long the ride takes.
A simple traveler line for naming your destination.
In traveler small talk or to a driver, you say where you are going.
Voy is the I-form of ir. Spanish uses it for I go and for near-future movement, like I am going to the station.
A sidewalk beside a taxi door, with a short destination line to the driver.
Before or during a ride, ask the duration.
A short question about the length of a ride or route.
Before or during the ride, you ask the driver or staff how long it takes.
Tarda is the time word in cuánto se tarda. It asks about duration, not clock time.
A quick look at a watch, then a calm question to the driver.
Stepping out of a taxi or train, announce arrival politely.
I am here now. All good.
A warm closing line after arriving safely.
I am here now. All good.
As you get out of the taxi or train, you briefly say you have arrived and all is fine.
Aquí means here and anchors the simple arrival phrase ya estoy aquí.
A taxi door opening at arrival, a calm thank-you moment, and soft city light.
Hotel, rooms, and simple guest needs
At a hotel front desk, open check-in by stating you have a reservation.
You ask for a room without a booking.
A short hotel check-in line that points to your reservation.
At the hotel front desk, you say that there is a reservation in your name.
Habitación is the hotel room word in Spain. It is more natural than cuarto for a hotel room.
A hotel front desk in warm evening light, with a suitcase beside the counter.
Hotel, rooms, and simple guest needs
As a walk-in at a hotel, ask for a room for tonight.
You ask which floor your room is on.
A polite walk-in request for a room without a prior booking.
At the front desk, you ask whether a room is free for tonight.
Noche can mean night or evening. In a hotel, esta noche clearly means tonight.
A late-evening reception desk, warm light, and a quick look at the booking list.
Hotel, rooms, and simple guest needs
After check-in, ask where your room is.
You ask for the room key.
Which floor is my room on?
A short orientation question after checking in.
Which floor is my room on?
After check-in, you take the key and ask which floor your room is on.
Piso means floor in this hotel context. In Spain it can also mean apartment, so context matters.
A key card at the front desk and a glance toward the elevator doors.
Hotel, rooms, and simple guest needs
At the front desk, ask politely for the room key.
You ask whether Wi-Fi is available.
A brief polite request for the room key.
At the front desk, you briefly and politely ask for the room key.
Llave means key. It can still be used around modern hotel key cards, especially as tarjeta-llave.
A key or card being passed across the counter in warm lobby light.
Hotel, rooms, and simple guest needs
At a hotel lobby or café, ask whether there is Wi-Fi.
You ask where the bathroom is.
A short question about Wi-Fi availability.
At the lobby or counter, you ask whether Wi-Fi is available here.
